title: Think Clearly
tagline: Catch your brain's shortcuts, spot bad info, and make better calls.
description: Learn the mental shortcuts that trip up smart people, how to take apart a bad argument, how to check a claim (or an AI fake) in under a minute, the few numbers ideas that protect you from scary headlines and bad deals, and simple tools for making big decisions.

units.title: Your Brain's Shortcuts
units.description: Cognitive biases: the predictable ways quick thinking goes wrong, and simple fixes.

levels.title: Confirmation Bias
levels.summary: We look for proof that we are right. Here is how to look for proof that you are wrong.

steps.title: Shortcuts that misfire
steps.body:
Your brain makes thousands of quick judgments a day. Most of the time its shortcuts work. Sometimes they misfire in predictable ways. Psychologists call these **cognitive biases**.

Biases are not a sign of low intelligence. Smart people have them too, and are sometimes better at defending them.

The most common one is **confirmation bias**: we notice, search for and remember information that supports what we already believe, and we brush off what does not.

steps.prompt: You think a new phone brand is junk. Which behavior shows confirmation bias?
options: Reading a mix of positive and negative reviews before deciding
Searching 'why brand X phones are bad' and sharing the first article that agrees with you
Asking a friend who owns one how it has held up
Checking a site that tests failure rates across many phones
steps.explain: The search itself was built to find agreement. A neutral search ('brand X phone reliability') or data from many users is far more likely to show the real picture.

steps.title: How it sneaks in
steps.body:
- **What you search for:** 'Is coffee bad for you?' finds different pages than 'benefits of coffee.'
- **How you judge evidence:** a study you like seems solid; one you dislike seems flawed.
- **What you remember:** you recall the hits and forget the misses ('I just knew it would rain!').
- **Who you follow:** feeds learn what you agree with and show you more of it.

> The fix is not to have no opinions. It is to go looking for the best case *against* your view on purpose.

steps.prompt: If you are very smart and well-informed, you are basically immune to confirmation bias.
steps.explain: Intelligence does not switch the bias off. Knowledgeable people can be even better at finding reasons to dismiss evidence they dislike. Habits like seeking out the other side protect you better than raw brainpower.

steps.prompt: Which habits help fight confirmation bias? Select all that apply.
options: Asking 'What would change my mind?' before looking at evidence
Searching with neutral terms rather than loaded ones
Only following accounts that share your values so you stay informed
Reading the strongest version of the opposing argument
Deciding first, then looking for support
steps.explain: Decide what evidence would matter before you look, search neutrally, and engage with the best opposing case. Echo chambers and decide-then-justify are confirmation bias in action.

steps.prompt: You are sure your favorite team's star player is the best in the league. A friend sends stats suggesting another player is better. What is the most clear-thinking reply?

options.text: 'Interesting. Before I argue, which stats do you think matter most? Let me look at those for both players.'
options.feedback: You agree on what counts as evidence first, then look. That is exactly how to beat confirmation bias, and it keeps the conversation fun instead of a fight.

options.text: 'Stats don't tell the whole story.' (then ignore them)
options.feedback: Sometimes true, but used here as a way to dismiss any evidence you dislike.

options.text: 'Your stats site is biased.'
options.feedback: Possible, but you have not checked. Attacking the source without looking is a common escape hatch.

options.text: Send back three highlight videos of your player.
options.feedback: Highlights are hand-picked best moments, which is the opposite of a fair comparison.

steps.explain: Agree on the measuring stick before you measure. If the evidence then goes against you, updating your view is a win for your thinking, not a loss.

steps.title: The 'consider the opposite' trick
steps.body:
Researchers have found a simple prompt reduces biased judgments: **ask yourself why your view might be wrong**, then list a few specific reasons.

Try it on a belief you hold strongly:
1. State the belief.
2. List 2-3 real reasons someone smart might disagree.
3. Ask what evidence would change your mind.
4. Go look for that evidence.

You may end up just as sure, but now for better reasons.

steps.prompt: Put the 'consider the opposite' routine in order.
items: State the belief clearly
List reasons a smart person might disagree
Decide what evidence would change your mind
Look for that evidence with neutral searches
Update your confidence based on what you find
steps.explain: Defining the test before you look is the key move. Otherwise you will tend to accept whatever you find as support.

steps.prompt: Pick one opinion you hold strongly (about a product, a person, a sports team, a habit). Write the best argument against it. What evidence would change your mind?
steps.placeholder: Belief: ... Best counterargument: ... What would change my mind: ...

levels.title: Sunk Costs, Anchors and Vivid Stories
levels.summary: Three biases that affect money and time decisions every week.

steps.title: Sunk cost: throwing good after bad
steps.body:
A **sunk cost** is time, money or effort already spent that you cannot get back. The **sunk cost fallacy** is letting it push you to keep going when stopping would be better.

- Sitting through a terrible movie because you paid for the ticket.
- Staying in a club you hate because you have been in it two years.
- Pouring money into a car that keeps breaking.

The ticket money is gone either way. The only real question is: **from now on, which choice is better?**

steps.prompt: You paid $60 for a concert ticket. On the day, you feel sick and a storm is coming, and you'd honestly rather stay home. Your friend isn't going anymore. What is the clearest reasoning?

options.text: 'The $60 is spent either way. Would I go if the ticket were free? No. So I'll try to resell it and stay home.'
options.feedback: This ignores the sunk cost and asks what is best from now on. Trying to resell it recovers some value too.

options.text: 'I paid $60, so I have to go or I wasted it.'
options.feedback: Classic sunk cost. Going while sick does not get the $60 back; it just adds a bad evening.

options.text: 'I'll go but leave after one song, so at least I used it.'
options.feedback: A compromise that still lets the spent money decide. If you do not want to go, the one song does not change the $60.

steps.explain: Imagine you never spent the money. If you would not choose it fresh, past spending is not a good reason to continue.

steps.title: Anchoring: the first number sticks
steps.body:
In a famous 1974 experiment, people spun a wheel that landed on 10 or 65, then guessed what percentage of UN countries were in Africa. Those who saw 10 guessed about 25%. Those who saw 65 guessed about 45%. A random number pulled their estimates.

**Anchoring** shows up everywhere: a 'was $200, now $99' tag, the first offer in a negotiation, a car's sticker price.

Fix: before seeing a number, decide your own estimate or limit. Research what similar things actually cost.

steps.prompt: An anchor only affects people when it is a believable number related to the question.
steps.explain: In the wheel experiment, everyone knew the number was random and unrelated, yet it still shifted their guesses. Obviously irrelevant anchors can still pull estimates.

steps.title: Availability: vivid beats common
steps.body:
We judge how likely something is by **how easily examples come to mind**. Dramatic, recent or heavily covered events feel more common than they are.

Shark attacks, plane crashes and kidnappings by strangers get huge coverage but are rare. Heart disease, car crashes and falls get little coverage but kill far more people.

Fix: when something feels likely or scary, ask **'How often does this actually happen?'** and look up the base numbers.

steps.prompt: Match each situation to the bias it shows.
pairs: Finishing a boring 900-page book because you're already halfway
Sunk cost fallacy
Thinking a used car is a deal because it's $3,000 below the sticker price
Anchoring
Being afraid to fly after seeing news of one crash, but texting while driving
Availability
Only reading reviews that agree with what you already decided to buy
Confirmation bias
steps.explain: Sunk cost looks backward at what you spent. Anchoring is being pulled by the first number. Availability is judging by what comes to mind easily. Confirmation bias is filtering for agreement.

steps.prompt: A store marks a jacket 'Was $180, NOW $90!' What is the best way to avoid being anchored?
options: Buy it, since half off is always a good deal
Ask: would I pay $90 for this jacket if I had never seen $180? Compare with similar jackets
Wait for it to drop to $45, since it was already cut in half once
Assume the $180 price was fake and the jacket is worth nothing
steps.explain: The 'was' price is an anchor. The real question is whether the jacket is worth $90 to you compared with alternatives. Assuming it is worthless swings too far the other way.

steps.prompt: Which are good questions to escape a sunk cost? Select all that apply.
options: If I were starting fresh today, would I choose this?
How much have I already put in?
What will the next hour, dollar or month get me here versus elsewhere?
What would I tell a friend in my position?
How bad will I feel about the money I already spent?
steps.explain: Good questions look forward and get outside your own head. Focusing on what you already spent or how bad the loss feels is what keeps the fallacy going.

steps.prompt: Is there something you are continuing mostly because of what you already put in (a game, a class, a hobby, a subscription, a project)? Apply the 'starting fresh today' test.
steps.placeholder: Thing: ... Already spent: ... Would I choose it fresh? ... Decision: ...

levels.title: Overconfidence and the Planning Fallacy
levels.summary: Why everything takes longer than planned, and how to estimate better.

steps.title: Too sure, too often
steps.body:
**Overconfidence** means being more sure than the evidence justifies. In many studies, when people say they are '90% sure,' they turn out to be right much less than 90% of the time.

It shows up as:
- Thinking you are a better-than-average driver (most people do)
- Being certain you will remember something without writing it down
- Narrow guesses: 'It'll cost exactly $500.'

Overconfidence makes you skip the backup plan.

steps.title: The planning fallacy
steps.body:
A special case: we underestimate how long our own tasks will take, even when we know similar tasks ran late before.

In a 1994 study, students predicted they would finish their senior thesis in about 34 days on average. It actually took them about 56 days. Fewer than a third finished by the time they predicted.

Why: we imagine the best-case path and forget interruptions, illness, waiting on others and the parts we haven't thought of yet.

source.label: Buehler, Griffin and Ross (1994), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

steps.prompt: Thinking through every step of your plan in more detail reliably fixes the planning fallacy.
steps.explain: Detailed step-by-step plans can still assume everything goes smoothly. A stronger fix is the outside view: check how long similar past tasks actually took, then plan with that.

steps.title: Use the outside view
steps.body:
The **inside view** asks: how long should *this* take, given my plan?

The **outside view** asks: how long did *things like this* take before, for me or others?

Simple method:
1. Make your estimate.
2. Check your track record: how much did past similar tasks overrun?
3. Multiply by that factor, or add a buffer.

> If you have no data, many people use a rough buffer of 1.5x for familiar tasks and 2x or more for new ones. Then track the real time so next time you have data.

steps.prompt: Your last 4 school projects took 1.5 times as long as you estimated. You estimate a new similar project will take 8 hours. Using your track record, how many hours should you plan for?
steps.explain: 8 hours x 1.5 = 12 hours. Planning 12 hours (and starting earlier) is more realistic than trusting your 8-hour inside-view estimate.

steps.prompt: Your boss at your part-time job asks how long it will take to reorganize the stockroom. Your gut says 2 hours. Last time a similar job took you nearly 4. What do you say?

options.text: 'My first guess is 2 hours, but the last one took about 4, so let's plan for 3 to 4. I'll update you halfway.'
options.feedback: Honest, uses your track record, and gives a check-in point. Bosses usually prefer a realistic estimate over a hopeful one that slips.

options.text: '2 hours, no problem.'
options.feedback: Sounds confident, but your own history says it is likely to run long, which hurts trust when it does.

options.text: 'I have no idea, could be anything.'
options.feedback: Too vague to be useful. You do have data: the last job.

options.text: 'Probably 8 hours, to be safe.'
options.feedback: Over-padding by a lot can look like you are slow or stalling. Use your real track record.

steps.explain: Give a range based on past results, not just your best-case picture, and offer an update along the way.

steps.prompt: Which are signs of overconfidence? Select all that apply.
options: 'I don't need to save this file, I'll remember the changes.'
'I'd say 60% likely, but I could be wrong.'
'This will definitely take 20 minutes, max.'
'Let me check how long it took last time.'
'I'll skip the practice test, I know this cold.'
steps.explain: Absolute certainty and skipping checks are red flags. Giving a probability and checking past data are signs of well-calibrated thinking.

steps.prompt: Order these steps for making a realistic time estimate.
items: Make your gut estimate
Look up how long similar past tasks took
Adjust your estimate using that track record
Add a buffer for unknowns and interruptions
Afterward, record the actual time for next time
steps.explain: Gut first, then reality check, adjust, buffer, and record. Recording actual time is what makes your future estimates better.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Being sure is a feeling, not evidence. Put a rough percentage on big beliefs.
- Your own tasks will usually take longer than your best-case picture.
- Use the outside view: what happened with similar tasks before?
- Track actual times to build your own data.

**This week:** before three tasks, write down how long you think each will take. Afterward, write how long it really took. Find your personal overrun factor.

units.title: Spot Bad Arguments and Bad Info
units.description: Recognize logical fallacies, check sources the way professional fact-checkers do, and avoid AI fakes and scams.

levels.title: Common Logical Fallacies
levels.summary: Name the tricks that make weak arguments sound strong.

steps.title: What is a fallacy?
steps.body:
A **logical fallacy** is a flaw in reasoning: the argument might sound convincing, but the conclusion does not actually follow from the reasons.

Knowing their names helps you notice them, in other people's arguments and in your own.

One warning before we start: a bad argument for a claim does not prove the claim is false. That mistake has a name too: the **fallacy fallacy**.

steps.title: Five you'll hear this week
steps.body:
- **Ad hominem:** attacking the person instead of the argument. 'You're 16, what do you know about taxes?'
- **Straw man:** twisting someone's view into a weaker version, then attacking that. 'You want less homework? So you want kids to learn nothing?'
- **False dilemma:** pretending there are only two options. 'Either you're with us or against us.'
- **Slippery slope:** claiming one step must lead to disaster with no evidence for each step.
- **Bandwagon:** 'Everyone's doing it, so it must be right.'

steps.prompt: Match each statement to the fallacy it uses.
pairs: 'Don't listen to her climate argument, she flies on planes.'
Ad hominem
'So you think we should just let everyone do whatever they want?'
Straw man
'Either you buy the premium plan or you don't care about security.'
False dilemma
'If we let you stay out till 11, next you'll be out all night every night.'
Slippery slope
'Millions of people use this supplement, so it must work.'
Bandwagon
steps.explain: Each one swaps a real reason for a shortcut: attacking the person, distorting the view, hiding other options, predicting an unsupported chain of events, or pointing to popularity.

steps.prompt: If someone uses a fallacy to argue for a claim, that proves the claim is false.
steps.explain: That is the fallacy fallacy. A person can argue badly for something true. A fallacy only tells you this particular argument does not support the conclusion; you need other evidence to decide.

steps.title: Is every slope slippery?
steps.body:
Not every 'this could lead to that' argument is a fallacy. It depends on whether there is **evidence for each link** in the chain.

- Fallacy: 'If you skip one workout, you'll end up never exercising again.'
- Reasonable: 'If you skip workouts whenever you're tired, it gets easier to skip next time, and habits fade.' (There is evidence that habits weaken without repetition.)

Ask: **how likely is each step, really?**

steps.prompt: In a class debate about school start times, an opponent says: 'My opponent only wants later start times because he's lazy.' It's your turn. What's the strongest response?

options.text: 'Whether I'm lazy or not doesn't change the evidence. Studies on teen sleep suggest later starts help. Can you respond to that evidence?'
options.feedback: You name the issue calmly without insult and steer back to the actual argument. Judges and audiences respect that.

options.text: 'Well, you're just a teacher's pet who wants to look good.'
options.feedback: Answering an ad hominem with another ad hominem makes you look just as weak.

options.text: 'That's an ad hominem fallacy! I win!'
options.feedback: Naming it is fine, but declaring victory is not an argument. You still need to make your case.

options.text: Say nothing about it and move on.
options.feedback: Not terrible, but the attack may stick with the audience. A one-line redirect is stronger.

steps.explain: Point out that the attack does not address the reasons, then restate your evidence. Calm beats clever.

steps.prompt: Which statement is a false dilemma?
options: 'We could take the bus, carpool, or bike. Which works best?'
'If you don't go to a 4-year college, you'll never have a good career.'
'This plan costs more upfront but less over 5 years.'
'Most studies so far show a small effect, but more research is needed.'
steps.explain: It ignores many real paths: trade schools, apprenticeships, community college, certifications and more. The other statements list options or describe evidence fairly.

steps.prompt: Which of these are fallacies rather than fair points? Select all that apply.
options: 'You can't trust his math, he dresses badly.'
'This doctor's advice conflicts with large studies, so let's look at the studies.'
'Every cool person has this sneaker, so you need it.'
'Either we ban phones totally or school is pointless.'
'The plan failed in three other towns for reasons that apply here too.'
steps.explain: Ad hominem, bandwagon and false dilemma. Checking advice against big studies and learning from similar cases are fair reasoning.

steps.prompt: This week, notice one fallacy in an ad, a comment section, a debate, or your own thinking. Write it down and name it. How could the argument be made fairly?
steps.placeholder: Where I saw it: ... Fallacy: ... Fair version: ...

levels.title: Check It Like a Fact-Checker
levels.summary: Lateral reading and the SIFT method: verify a claim in under a minute.

steps.title: What the pros do differently
steps.body:
Stanford researchers watched three groups judge websites: history professors, college students, and professional fact-checkers. The fact-checkers were faster and much more accurate.

Their secret: they **left the page almost immediately**. Instead of reading the 'About us' page or judging the design, they opened new tabs and searched what *other* sources said about the site and its claim.

This is called **lateral reading**: reading across, not down.

source.label: Stanford News on Wineburg and McGrew (2017)

steps.prompt: A website with a professional design, a .org address, and a detailed 'About us' page is probably trustworthy.
steps.explain: Anyone can buy a .org domain and a nice template, and an organization will describe itself favorably. In the Stanford study, these cues fooled professors and students. What others say about the source tells you much more.

steps.title: SIFT: four moves
steps.body:
Digital literacy expert Mike Caulfield's **SIFT** method:

- **S - Stop.** Notice your emotional reaction. Do you know this source?
- **I - Investigate the source.** Search the site or person's name in a new tab. Who are they? What do others say?
- **F - Find better coverage.** Search the claim itself. Do trusted outlets or fact-checkers report it?
- **T - Trace to the original.** Find the original study, video or quote. Was it cut, changed, or taken out of context?

Most checks take under a minute.

steps.prompt: Put the SIFT moves in order.
items: Stop and notice your reaction before sharing
Investigate who is behind the source
Find better coverage of the same claim
Trace the claim back to its original context
steps.explain: Stop, Investigate, Find, Trace. Stopping comes first because strong emotions are what make people share without checking.

steps.prompt: Your aunt posts a screenshot: 'NEW STUDY: Popular cereal causes memory loss in kids!' from a site you've never heard of. She asks the family to share it. What do you do?

options.text: Search the claim and the site's name. If no major outlet or the actual study backs it, reply privately: 'I looked this up and couldn't find the study. Here's what I found instead. Might be worth holding off on sharing.'
options.feedback: You checked laterally, then corrected privately and kindly with something better to look at. People are less defensive when they are not called out in public.

options.text: Comment publicly: 'This is fake news, do some research.'
options.feedback: Even if it is false, a public put-down makes people dig in. And you have not shown what is true.

options.text: Share it just in case it's true.
options.feedback: Sharing unchecked scary claims spreads misinformation. 'Just in case' is how false claims go viral.

options.text: Read the whole article carefully to decide if it sounds believable.
options.feedback: Reading 'down' the page tells you how convincing it sounds, not whether it is true. Check what other sources say.

steps.explain: Check laterally first, then correct gently and privately, and offer a better source rather than just saying 'wrong.'

steps.prompt: Which are lateral reading moves? Select all that apply.
options: Searching the website's name plus 'funding' or 'bias' in a new tab
Reading the site's own 'About us' page carefully
Checking whether a fact-checking site has covered the claim
Looking up the author on other sites
Judging how professional the website looks
steps.explain: Lateral reading means leaving the page to see what independent sources say. The 'About us' page and design are on the page itself, and easy to fake.

steps.prompt: A viral video shows a politician saying something shocking. The clip is 8 seconds long. Which SIFT move matters most here?
options: Stop: decide how angry it makes you
Trace: find the full original video to see the context
Investigate: check how many views the clip has
Find: count how many friends shared it
steps.explain: Short clips are easy to cut so they mean the opposite of what was said. Finding the full original is the key check. View and share counts say nothing about accuracy.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Do not judge a source by its looks or its own description.
- Leave the page: search what others say about the source and the claim.
- Use SIFT: Stop, Investigate, Find better coverage, Trace to the original.
- Correct friends and family privately and kindly, with a better source.

**This week:** the next time a post makes you feel shocked or angry, spend 60 seconds on SIFT before reacting or sharing.

levels.title: Misinformation Tricks and AI Fakes
levels.summary: Spot manipulation techniques, AI-generated images and voice-clone scams.

steps.title: Know the tricks in advance
steps.body:
Researchers have found that learning how manipulation works *before* you meet it makes you better at spotting it. It is called **prebunking**, like a vaccine for misinformation.

In studies with short videos, including one shown as YouTube ads to real users, people who watched got better at recognizing these techniques:
- **Emotional language:** outrage and fear words to make you react, not think
- **False dilemmas:** only two choices
- **Scapegoating:** blaming one group for a complex problem
- **Ad hominem:** attacking the person instead of the argument

Another common trick: **fake experts**, people with impressive titles speaking outside their field.

steps.prompt: Match each headline to the manipulation technique it uses.
pairs: 'SHOCKING: What they're hiding in your tap water will TERRIFY you'
Emotional language
'Rising rents are all the fault of one immigrant group'
Scapegoating
'A doctor says vaccines are dangerous' (he's a retired dentist)
Fake expert
'Either we ban all cars or the planet is doomed'
False dilemma
steps.explain: Each technique pushes a reaction while skipping real evidence. Spotting the technique is a signal to slow down and check.

steps.title: AI-generated images and video
steps.body:
AI can now create realistic faces, photos and video. In a 2022 study, people trying to tell real faces from AI faces were right only **48%** of the time, no better than flipping a coin. Training raised it to about 59%. The AI faces were even rated slightly **more trustworthy** than real ones.

So the old advice to 'look for weird hands' is not reliable anymore. Better checks:
- Trace it: who posted it first? Is there a credible original source?
- Reverse image search it.
- Check if reliable outlets report the event.

steps.prompt: Most people can reliably tell AI-generated faces from real photos if they look closely.
steps.explain: In the 2022 study, untrained people scored about 48%, around chance. Even with tips, accuracy only reached about 59%. Checking the source beats squinting at pixels.

steps.title: Voice clones and family emergency scams
steps.body:
Scammers can clone a voice from a short clip posted online. A common scam: a call that sounds like a family member in trouble ('I've been in an accident, I need money now, don't tell Mom').

The US Federal Trade Commission advises:
- **Hang up and call the person back** on a number you already know.
- Be suspicious of urgency, secrecy, and requests for gift cards, wire transfers or crypto.
- Many families agree on a **code word** to verify emergencies.

source.label: FTC Consumer Alert on AI family emergency scams

steps.prompt: You get a call. It sounds exactly like your brother, crying: 'I'm in trouble, I need $500 in gift cards right now, please don't tell anyone.' What do you do?

options.text: Say 'I'll call you right back,' hang up, and call your brother's real number (or a parent). Ask for your family code word if you have one.
options.feedback: Exactly right. A real emergency survives a 1-minute callback. A scam usually falls apart.

options.text: Buy the gift cards fast, since it's clearly his voice.
options.feedback: Voices can be cloned. Gift cards, urgency and secrecy are three classic scam signs together.

options.text: Ask him a few personal questions on the same call.
options.feedback: Better than nothing, but scammers may know details from social media. Calling back on a known number is much safer.

options.text: Keep him talking and promise to send money later.
options.feedback: This keeps you in the scammer's script. End the call and verify independently.

steps.explain: Urgency + secrecy + unusual payment = scam until proven otherwise. Verify through a separate channel you trust.

steps.title: AI chatbots: useful, not an oracle
steps.body:
AI chatbots are great for explaining ideas and brainstorming, but they can state wrong things confidently, including **made-up quotes, statistics and sources**.

- For facts that matter (health, money, legal, school citations), **check the claim in a reliable source**.
- If a chatbot gives a source, open it. Make sure it exists and says what was claimed.
- AI text detectors are unreliable and can wrongly flag human writing, so do not treat them as proof either way.

steps.prompt: Which are red flags that a message or post may be a scam or manipulation? Select all that apply.
options: Pressure to act right now
A request to pay with gift cards or crypto
A link to the full original source you can check
A demand to keep it secret
Lots of outrage words in all caps
steps.explain: Urgency, unusual payments, secrecy and emotional overload are classic signs. A checkable original source is a good sign, though you should still check it.

steps.prompt: Talk with your family this week: agree on a code word for real emergencies, and on a rule to call back on known numbers. What is your plan?
steps.placeholder: e.g. Talk to parents Sunday at dinner, pick a code word, save each other's numbers...

units.title: Numbers That Don't Fool You
units.description: Base rates, risk percentages, correlation and expected value: the math that protects you from bad headlines and bad deals.

levels.title: Base Rates
levels.summary: Why a positive test result often means less than you think.

steps.title: Start with how common it is
steps.body:
The **base rate** is how common something is in the first place. People tend to ignore it and focus on the vivid details in front of them.

Example: a quiet guy who loves reading. Is he more likely a librarian or a salesperson? Many say librarian. But there are far more salespeople than librarians in the US, so even if only a few salespeople are bookish, there could be more bookish salespeople than librarians in total.

Always ask: **out of how many?**

steps.title: Count people, not percentages
steps.body:
Percentages get confusing fast. Researchers found that people reason much better when the same information is written as **counts of people** (natural frequencies).

Imagine a disease that 1 in 100 people have. A test catches 90% of people who have it. But it also wrongly flags 10% of healthy people.

Picture **1,000 people**:
- 10 have the disease. The test catches **9** of them.
- 990 are healthy. The test wrongly flags 10% of them: **99** people.

steps.prompt: Using those 1,000 people: 9 sick people test positive and 99 healthy people test positive. How many people in total test positive?
steps.explain: 9 true positives + 99 false positives = 108 positive results.

steps.prompt: Of those 108 people who tested positive, only 9 are actually sick. What percent of positive results are real cases? (Round to the nearest whole number.)
steps.explain: 9 / 108 = 0.083, about 8%. So even with a test that catches 90% of cases, a positive result here means only about an 8% chance of having the disease, because the disease is rare and false alarms outnumber real cases.

steps.prompt: If a test is '90% accurate' and you test positive, there is a 90% chance you have the condition.
steps.explain: It depends on how common the condition is. For rare conditions, false positives among the many healthy people can outnumber true positives, as in the example where the real chance was about 8%. That is why doctors often confirm with a second test.

steps.prompt: Your friend took an online screening quiz and got a result saying they 'likely have' a rare condition. They are panicking. What is the best thing to say?

options.text: 'That's scary, I get it. Screening tools flag lots of people who turn out fine, especially for rare things. A doctor can do a proper check. Want help making an appointment?'
options.feedback: You take the feeling seriously, explain base rates in plain words, and point to a real next step.

options.text: 'Online quizzes are always garbage, ignore it.'
options.feedback: Dismissive. Some screening tools are useful, and if your friend has symptoms, a check is still worth it.

options.text: 'Wow, if the quiz says so, you probably have it.'
options.feedback: This ignores the base rate and adds to the panic.

options.text: 'Look up the condition and read about the worst cases.'
options.feedback: This makes the worst case feel more likely (availability bias) without telling you anything about your friend's actual chance.

steps.explain: A positive screen for something rare is a reason to get properly checked, not proof. Calm, plus a concrete next step.

steps.prompt: A security system flags suspicious bags at a stadium. It flags 99% of bags with weapons and 1% of normal bags. Out of 100,000 bags, 1 contains a weapon. About how many flagged bags are normal?
options: About 1
About 10
About 1,000
About 99,000
steps.explain: 1% of the 99,999 normal bags is about 1,000 false alarms, versus about 1 real weapon. So almost every flagged bag is normal, which is why a flag leads to a second check, not an arrest.

steps.prompt: Order the steps to figure out what a positive test really means.
items: Pick a round group size, like 1,000 people
Use the base rate to find how many actually have it
Find how many of those the test catches
Find how many healthy people get a false positive
Divide true positives by all positives
steps.explain: Turning percentages into counts of people makes the answer almost obvious. True positives divided by everyone who tested positive is the real chance.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Always ask how common something is to begin with.
- Convert percentages into counts of people (out of 1,000 or 10,000).
- For rare things, even good tests produce many false alarms.
- A positive screening result usually means 'check further,' not 'definitely yes.'

**This week:** when you see a claim like 'X% accurate' or 'flags Y%,' rewrite it as 'out of 1,000 people...' and see what changes.

levels.title: Scary Headlines: Risk and Causation
levels.summary: Relative vs absolute risk, and why correlation is not causation.

steps.title: 'Doubles your risk!' Of what?
steps.body:
A headline says something 'doubles your risk.' That is **relative risk**: compared with before. It does not tell you how big the risk is.

- If a risk goes from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000, it **doubled**. But the extra risk is **1 person in 10,000**.
- If a risk goes from 10 in 100 to 20 in 100, it also doubled, and that is 10 extra people per 100.

The second is a much bigger deal. Always ask for the **absolute risk**: how many out of how many, before and after?

steps.prompt: A news story says a habit 'raises your risk of a rare illness by 50%.' The normal risk is 4 in 10,000 people. How many people per 10,000 would get the illness with the habit?
steps.explain: 50% of 4 is 2. So 4 + 2 = 6 in 10,000. The scary '50%' means 2 extra people out of every 10,000.

steps.title: When relative risk causes real harm
steps.body:
In 1995, UK health officials warned that some newer birth control pills **doubled** the risk of dangerous blood clots. In absolute terms the risk was still very small. Many women stopped taking the pill suddenly.

Researchers later found that unplanned pregnancies and abortions rose after the scare. Pregnancy itself carries a higher clot risk than those pills did.

> The lesson: a scary relative number with no absolute number can push people into worse choices.

source.label: Del Bono, Furnari and Ermisch (2011), ISER working paper on the 1995 pill scare

steps.prompt: If a news story reports only that something 'increases risk by 200%,' you have enough information to know if you should worry.
steps.explain: You need the starting risk. A 200% increase on 1 in a million is still tiny (3 in a million). On 1 in 10 it would be huge (3 in 10).

steps.title: Correlation is not causation
steps.body:
Two things moving together (**correlation**) does not mean one causes the other.

- **Third factor:** ice cream sales and drownings rise together. Both are caused by hot weather.
- **Reverse direction:** people who sleep with the TV on are more tired. Maybe tired, stressed people are the ones who leave the TV on.
- **Coincidence:** with enough data, random things line up.

The strongest evidence for causation usually comes from **randomized experiments**, where chance decides who gets the treatment.

steps.prompt: Match each claim to the most likely problem with it.
pairs: Kids with more books at home get better grades, so buying books raises grades
A third factor (like family income or reading habits) may explain both
People who use fitness trackers are healthier, so trackers make you healthy
Reverse direction: healthy people may be more likely to buy trackers
My lucky socks work: I wore them and we won 3 games
Coincidence and a tiny sample
In a randomized trial, the group given the drug recovered faster
Good evidence of cause, if the trial was well run
steps.explain: Third factors, reverse causation and small samples explain many headline correlations. Randomized trials are designed to rule these out.

steps.prompt: Your friend sends you a headline: 'Study: Teens who eat breakfast get better grades.' He says: 'So if I eat breakfast I'll get better grades!' What's the clearest reply?

options.text: 'Could be, but it might be that kids with more structured mornings or more sleep do both. Breakfast is still a good idea, just don't expect it alone to fix grades.'
options.feedback: You point out the possible third factor without being a buzzkill, and keep the useful advice.

options.text: 'Correlation isn't causation, so the study is worthless.'
options.feedback: Correlation studies are not worthless; they suggest what to test. The problem is only jumping straight to cause.

options.text: 'Yep, science proves it.'
options.feedback: An observational study like this cannot show breakfast is the cause on its own.

steps.explain: Ask what else could explain the link. Correlations are useful clues, not proof.

steps.prompt: Which questions should you ask about a scary health headline? Select all that apply.
options: What is the absolute risk before and after?
Was it a randomized experiment or an observational study?
How many shares has the story gotten?
Could a third factor explain the link?
Was the study done in people or only in mice or cells?
steps.explain: Absolute numbers, study type, possible confounders and who was studied all matter. Share counts tell you about popularity, not truth.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- 'Doubles your risk' means nothing without the starting number. Ask: how many out of how many?
- Correlation can come from a third factor, reverse direction or chance.
- Randomized experiments are the best evidence of cause.
- Studies in mice or cells are early clues, not proof for humans.

**This week:** find one health or science headline and rewrite it with absolute numbers, or say what type of study it was.

levels.title: Expected Value
levels.summary: Weigh chances and payoffs to see which bets, deals and warranties are worth it.

steps.title: Average result over many tries
steps.body:
**Expected value** is what a choice is worth on average if you could repeat it many times.

Multiply each possible outcome by its chance, then add them up.

Example: a game costs $1. You have a 1 in 10 chance of winning $5.
- Expected winnings: 1/10 x $5 = $0.50
- Minus the cost: $0.50 - $1 = **-$0.50**

On average you lose 50 cents each time you play. Over 100 plays, expect to be down about $50.

steps.prompt: A school raffle ticket costs $5. There are 500 tickets sold and one prize of $1,000. What is the expected value of buying one ticket, after subtracting its cost? (Use a minus sign for a loss.)
steps.explain: Chance of winning = 1/500. Expected winnings = $1,000 / 500 = $2. Subtract the $5 cost: $2 - $5 = -$3. That is fine if you are happy to donate to the school, but it is not a money-making bet.

steps.title: Why casinos and lotteries always win
steps.body:
Casino games and lotteries are designed with **negative expected value** for players. Some people win, but on average, players lose and the house collects the difference.

The more you play, the closer your results get to that average. That is why 'I'm due for a win' is a trap: each spin or ticket is independent. Past losses do not make the next win more likely (that belief is called the **gambler's fallacy**).

steps.prompt: If a coin lands heads 6 times in a row, it is more likely to land tails next time.
steps.explain: A fair coin has no memory. The chance is still 50%. Believing otherwise is the gambler's fallacy, and it keeps people betting after losses.

steps.prompt: A store offers a $60 extended warranty on a $300 speaker. Suppose about 10% of these speakers break during the warranty period and the warranty would pay $300 for a replacement. What is the expected payout of the warranty, in dollars?
steps.explain: 10% x $300 = $30. You would pay $60 for an expected $30 of protection. That is why extended warranties are profitable for stores. Saving the $60 in an emergency fund is usually better, unless you truly could not afford a replacement.

steps.title: When expected value isn't everything
steps.body:
Expected value is about averages. Two things can matter more:

- **Can you survive the bad outcome?** Health insurance can have negative expected value in dollars but protects you from a bill you could never pay. That is worth it.
- **One-time vs repeated:** for a one-time huge decision, think about the worst case, not just the average.

Use expected value for small, repeated choices. For rare disasters, protect against ruin.

steps.prompt: A friend says: 'I spend $20 a week on scratch-off tickets. Someone won $50,000 last month at my store, so it's a smart investment.' What do you say?

options.text: 'Every ticket is designed so players lose money on average. $20 a week is over $1,000 a year. If you enjoy it as entertainment, maybe set a smaller limit, but it's not an investment.'
options.feedback: Clear, uses real numbers, and does not lecture about fun. It separates entertainment from investing.

options.text: 'Good idea, someone has to win.'
options.feedback: Someone does win, but the average player loses. One big winner is the availability bias at work.

options.text: 'You're an idiot for gambling.'
options.feedback: Insults make people defensive. Your friend is more likely to listen to the numbers.

steps.explain: Show the yearly cost and the negative expected value. Seeing a winner does not change the odds for everyone else.

steps.prompt: Match each choice to the best way to think about it.
pairs: Buying a lottery ticket every day
Negative expected value that adds up over time
Health insurance
Worth it to avoid a ruinous bill, even if it loses money on average
Extended warranty on cheap headphones
Usually negative expected value; you could afford to replace them
Index fund investing over 20 years
Historically positive expected value, though returns are not guaranteed
steps.explain: Expected value tells you the average. Also ask: could I survive the worst case, and am I doing this once or many times?

steps.prompt: Think of a recurring purchase or bet (games, loot boxes, tickets, warranties, subscriptions). Estimate its yearly cost and what you expect to get back. Is it worth it to you?
steps.placeholder: e.g. Loot boxes: $10 a week = $520 a year, for ...

units.title: Better Decisions
units.description: Tools for choosing well: opportunity cost, reversible vs irreversible choices, pre-mortems and second-order thinking.

levels.title: Opportunity Cost and Doors
levels.summary: Every choice costs the next best option. Some choices deserve speed, some deserve care.

steps.title: The hidden price tag
steps.body:
The **opportunity cost** of a choice is the best thing you give up to make it.

- Spending $800 on a new phone means not having $800 for a car repair, a trip, or savings.
- Spending 3 hours a night gaming means not spending them on sleep, a side job, or friends.

People often forget this. In one study, simply reminding shoppers that not buying an item would leave them money for other things made them noticeably less likely to buy. The alternatives were there all along; they just were not thinking about them.

steps.prompt: Jay can work 10 extra hours this weekend at $15 an hour or go on a camping trip that costs $50. What is the full cost of the trip, counting opportunity cost?
options: $0, because he enjoys it
steps.explain: $50 for the trip plus $150 of wages he gives up (10 x $15) = $200. The trip may still be worth it! Knowing the full cost just makes it a real choice.

steps.prompt: You spend $6 on drinks and snacks every school day. Assume 180 school days a year. How many dollars is that per year?
steps.explain: $6 x 180 = $1,080 a year. That is the opportunity cost to compare against other things you want, like a new laptop or savings.

steps.title: One-way and two-way doors
steps.body:
Some decisions are **two-way doors**: if it goes badly, you can walk back through. Trying a new club, a new haircut, a different study method. Decide fast, try it, adjust.

Others are **one-way doors**: hard or impossible to undo. Signing a long lease, taking a big loan, getting a tattoo, posting something you can't unpost. Slow down, gather information, sleep on it.

The mistake is treating every choice the same: agonizing over small reversible ones, or rushing big permanent ones.

steps.prompt: Match each decision to how to approach it.
pairs: Trying a new lunch spot
Two-way door: decide fast
Signing a 2-year phone contract with a big early cancellation fee
One-way door: slow down and compare
Testing a new morning routine for a week
Two-way door: experiment
Taking a $20,000 private student loan
One-way door: research carefully and get advice
steps.explain: Easy-to-reverse choices are cheap experiments. Hard-to-reverse ones deserve research, comparison and time.

steps.prompt: For most decisions, you should gather as much information as possible before choosing.
steps.explain: For reversible, low-stakes decisions, the time spent researching often costs more than a wrong choice would. Try it and adjust. Save deep research for decisions that are expensive or hard to undo.

steps.prompt: A salesperson at a car dealership says the 0% financing deal ends today, so you need to sign the 6-year loan now. You hadn't planned to buy today. What do you say?

options.text: 'Thanks, but I don't sign big contracts the same day. If the deal's gone tomorrow, I'll live with that.' Then walk out and compare offers at home.
options.feedback: A car loan is a one-way door. Pressure to decide today is a sales tactic, and a real good deal usually returns.

options.text: 'Okay, I don't want to miss out.'
options.feedback: Urgency is designed to make you skip comparison on an expensive, hard-to-reverse decision.

options.text: 'Can you give me 10 minutes to look at the paperwork here?'
options.feedback: Better than signing instantly, but you are still deciding under pressure in their space. Take the paperwork home.

steps.explain: Pressure to decide fast on a one-way door is a red flag. Slow down and compare outside the sales setting.

steps.prompt: Which of these are one-way doors that deserve extra care? Select all that apply.
options: Co-signing a loan for a friend
Trying a free week at a new gym
Posting an angry public comment about your employer
Picking a new phone wallpaper
Dropping out of a program with no option to return
steps.explain: Co-signing makes you legally responsible, public posts are hard to fully delete, and dropping out may not be reversible. A free trial and a wallpaper are easy to undo.

steps.prompt: Name one decision you are facing. Is it a one-way or two-way door? What is its opportunity cost? Based on that, how much time should you spend on it?
steps.placeholder: Decision: ... Door type: ... What I give up: ... Time to spend: ...

levels.title: Pre-Mortems and Second-Order Thinking
levels.summary: Imagine failure in advance, and ask 'and then what?'

steps.title: The pre-mortem
steps.body:
A post-mortem looks at why something failed after it happened. A **pre-mortem** does it in advance.

Psychologist Gary Klein's method:
1. Imagine it is months from now, and your plan **failed badly**.
2. Write down every reason it might have failed.
3. Fix or prepare for the biggest ones now.

Imagining the failure as already happened makes it easier to come up with reasons. In one study, this kind of 'looking back from the future' raised people's ability to correctly identify reasons for an outcome by about 30%.

source.label: Gary Klein, Performing a Project Premortem, Harvard Business Review (2007)

steps.prompt: Put the pre-mortem steps in order.
items: Describe the plan clearly
Imagine it is the future and the plan failed
List every reason it could have failed
Pick the most likely or most damaging reasons
Change the plan or add a backup for those
steps.explain: Plan, imagine failure, list causes, prioritize, then act. The point is to change the plan, not just worry.

steps.prompt: You and two friends plan to start a lawn-mowing business this summer. One of you suggests a pre-mortem. Which output is most useful?

options.text: 'It failed because: we couldn't get customers (fix: flyers in 3 neighborhoods by May), the mower broke (fix: set aside $100 for repairs), and someone quit (fix: agree on hours and pay split in writing).'
options.feedback: Specific failure reasons, each with a concrete fix. That is a pre-mortem doing its job.

options.text: 'It could fail, but let's stay positive.'
options.feedback: Positivity is nice, but it skips the whole point of the exercise.

options.text: 'It will probably fail, so let's not do it.'
options.feedback: A pre-mortem is for strengthening a plan, not for giving up on it.

options.text: 'Bad luck might happen.'
options.feedback: Too vague to act on. Name specific things that could go wrong.

steps.explain: Good pre-mortems name concrete causes and attach concrete fixes or backups.

steps.title: Second-order thinking: 'and then what?'
steps.body:
**First-order thinking** looks at the immediate result. **Second-order thinking** asks what happens after that.

- First order: 'Skipping sleep gives me 2 more hours to study.' Second order: 'Tomorrow I'm slower and remember less.'
- First order: 'Buy now, pay later makes it affordable.' Second order: 'Several small plans add up, and late fees can follow.'
- First order: 'Quitting my job feels great today.' Second order: 'How will I pay rent next month?'

Ask **'and then what?'** at least twice.

steps.prompt: A city makes downtown parking free to help local shops. What is a second-order effect to consider?
options: Parking becomes free
Drivers save money on parking
Spaces fill up early with all-day parkers, so shoppers can't find spots
The city sign says 'Free Parking'
steps.explain: The first-order effect is free parking. Second order: free spots get taken by commuters who stay all day, which can make it harder for shoppers to park, the opposite of the goal.

steps.prompt: Second-order effects always make a choice worse than it first looks.
steps.explain: Sometimes the later effects are good. Exercising is unpleasant at first but leads to more energy and better sleep. Second-order thinking just means looking further ahead, in both directions.

steps.prompt: You're thinking about leasing a new car at 18 with a low monthly payment. Which are second-order questions worth asking? Select all that apply.
options: What happens to my insurance cost as a young driver with a newer car?
What color do I want?
What if I drive more than the lease's mileage limit?
What if I move or want to end the lease early?
Will my friends like it?
steps.explain: Insurance, mileage penalties and early termination costs are later effects that can make a 'cheap' lease expensive. Color and friends' opinions are first-order preferences.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Before a big plan, run a pre-mortem: imagine it failed, list why, and fix the top reasons.
- Ask 'and then what?' at least twice for important choices.
- Later effects can be good or bad; look in both directions.

**This week:** run a 10-minute pre-mortem on one plan (a trip, a project, a purchase, a schedule). Write three failure reasons and one fix for each.

levels.title: A Decision Toolkit
levels.summary: Put it all together into a simple process for your big choices.

steps.title: A simple process for big choices
steps.body:
You won't run a full process for every choice. But for the big ones (a school, a job, a car, a move), a few steps help a lot:

1. **Frame it:** what exactly are you deciding, and by when?
2. **Widen options:** don't stop at 'yes or no.' Is there a third option?
3. **Check door type:** reversible or not?
4. **Gather the outside view:** what happened to others who chose each option?
5. **Pre-mortem** your top choice.
6. **Decide and set a review date.**

steps.prompt: Put the decision steps in order.
items: Frame the decision and the deadline
List more than two options
Check whether it is reversible
Look at what happened to others who made similar choices
Run a pre-mortem on your favorite
Decide and set a date to review
steps.explain: Framing and widening options come first, because a decision is only as good as the options you considered. Reviewing later is how you learn.

steps.title: Avoid the 'whether or not' trap
steps.body:
Decision researchers have noticed that people often frame choices as 'whether or not': Should I take this job or not? Should I buy this car or not?

That hides other options. Better: **'What are all the ways I could get what I want here?'**

- 'Should I quit my job?' becomes: 'Could I change shifts, talk to my manager, look for a new job while staying, or quit?'
- 'Should I buy a car?' becomes: 'Used car, transit pass, bike plus rideshare, or carpool?'

steps.prompt: Your brother says: 'Should I go to State University or not?' He feels stuck. Which reply helps him think most clearly?

options.text: 'What do you want out of the next few years? Let's list every path that could get you there: State, community college then transfer, a trade program, working for a year. Then compare costs and what happened to people who did each.'
options.feedback: You widen the options, anchor on his goals, and suggest the outside view. That turns a stuck yes/no into a real comparison.

options.text: 'Just go, everyone goes to college.'
options.feedback: That is the bandwagon fallacy, and it skips cost and fit, which matter a lot for a one-way-door choice.

options.text: 'Flip a coin.'
options.feedback: Fine for a small reversible choice, but this is expensive and hard to undo.

options.text: 'Don't go, college is a scam.'
options.feedback: Overconfident and one-sided. For many careers, a degree pays off. It depends on the program, cost and goals.

steps.explain: Turn 'whether or not' into 'which of several options,' tie it to goals, and look at real outcomes.

steps.prompt: Match each tool to when it helps most.
pairs: Pre-mortem
Before committing to a plan
Outside view
When estimating time, cost or chance of success
Opportunity cost
When spending money or time
Consider the opposite
When you feel very sure you're right
Natural frequencies
When interpreting test results or risk percentages
steps.explain: Each tool fixes a different weak spot: overconfidence in plans, optimistic estimates, invisible trade-offs, one-sided thinking and confusing percentages.

steps.prompt: If a decision turned out badly, it must have been a bad decision.
steps.explain: Good decisions can have bad luck, and bad decisions can get lucky. Judge a decision by the information and reasoning you had at the time. Poker players call mixing these up 'resulting.'

steps.prompt: Six months after choosing a summer job, you review the decision. Which question is most useful?
options: Did it turn out well? Then I'm a great decision-maker.
What did I know then, what did I miss, and what would I check next time?
Whose fault was it that it went badly?
How can I avoid ever making a decision like this again?
steps.explain: Reviewing your process (what you knew, what you missed) improves your next decision. Judging only by the outcome or by blame teaches the wrong lessons.

steps.prompt: Which habits make a decision process better? Select all that apply.
options: Writing down why you chose, so you can review later
Considering at least three options
Deciding big things right after a fight or bad news
Sleeping on one-way-door decisions
Only asking people who will agree with you
steps.explain: Writing your reasons, widening options and sleeping on big choices all help. Deciding while upset and asking only people who agree bring in emotion and confirmation bias.

steps.prompt: Pick a real decision in your life right now. Run the toolkit: frame it, list at least three options, check the door type, and do a 3-reason pre-mortem. When will you decide, and when will you review it?
steps.placeholder: Decision: ... Options: 1) 2) 3) ... Door: ... Pre-mortem: ... Decide by: ... Review on: ...
